name: Benzo Brown
lede: Benzo Brown is a muted taupe-brown from Ridgway's 1912 chart, called Aku-iro, lye-colored, in Japanese tradition, and the single most common of these twelve colors in our painting archive.

sections.title: A taupe called lye-colored
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 chart carries this brown on two plates, XLVI and XLV, both tone i, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files a close match in block 61 [1]. In Japan the same hue is called Aku-iro, written 灰汁色 and meaning lye-colored, after the alkaline ash-water once used in dyeing and cooking [1]. The library's closest recorded duplicate is Deep Brownish Drab, about 2.4 units away [1].

In LCH terms it measures lightness 49, chroma 10, hue 67 degrees, and the nearest everyday name on file is [[taupe]], about 5.4 units of ΔE away, a close match [1]. Among named neutrals it sits beside [[umber]] and [[sepia]], and shares its Japanese cross-reference with [[amber-brown]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this brown in 2,436 of 23,781 paintings, 10.2 percent, the most common of any color, as photographed [2]. The earliest dated match, a Chinese painting called The Kill, is dated to about 300 BCE in our archive, more than two thousand years before either the Ridgway chart or the Japanese name are recorded, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. It peaks around 1270, at 3.5 times the archive's overall rate, and the painter Shen Zhou carries it in eight of his twelve paintings here, two-thirds of his output [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone, in 49 percent of its appearances [2].

origin.named_after: undocumented beyond the chemical-sounding prefix benzo
